ops.old: The most comprehensive evaluation of MSSP clinical outcomes, published by CMS in 2025 using 12 years of program data, found that ACOs in their fifth year or beyond reduced preventable hospital admissions by 8.3% and emergency department visits for ambulatory-sensitive conditions by 11.4% relative to matched fee-for-service beneficiaries, after controlling for demographic and health status differences. These effects were concentrated in the chronic disease categories where effective primary care management has the strongest evidence base: diabetes (14.2% reduction in preventable admissions), congestive heart failure (18.7% reduction), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (12.4% reduction). Importantly, the quality improvement was not accompanied by evidence of care withholding: preventive screening completion rates, cancer screening rates, and chronic disease monitoring rates were all higher in mature ACO populations than in fee-for-service comparison groups, suggesting that the outcome improvements reflected better care management, not reduced care access.
ops.new: The most cited peer-reviewed evaluation of MSSP clinical and spending performance, by McWilliams and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine (2016), compared 220 ACOs with local non-ACO providers using Medicare claims. ACOs that entered in 2012 reduced spending by about $144 per beneficiary — roughly 1.4% — by 2013, while the 2013 entry cohort showed no significant savings in its first year, an early sign that savings take time to develop. Savings were consistently larger in independent primary care groups than in hospital-integrated ones. Importantly, the savings were not accompanied by evidence of care withholding: ACO contracts were associated with improved performance on some quality measures — including fewer hospitalizations for COPD and asthma — and unchanged performance on the rest, suggesting that the spending reductions reflected better care management, not reduced access.
ops.claim: CMS 2025 "MSSP 12-Year Evaluation" found mature ACOs cut preventable admissions 8.3%, ambulatory-sensitive ED visits 11.4%, diabetes 14.2%, CHF 18.7%, COPD 12.4%
ops.sources: McWilliams JM et al., "Early Performance of Accountable Care Organizations in Medicare," NEJM 2016;374:2357-66 (220 ACOs; 2012 cohort -$144/beneficiary, 1.4%, in 2013; 2013 cohort -$3, NS; improved on some quality measures, unchanged on others; savings greater in independent primary care groups)
ops.note: No CMS "MSSP 12-Year Evaluation Report" exists; all five percentages were invented. Replaced with the real peer-reviewed MSSP evaluation.

ops.old: A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP participation within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients, suggesting that the program’s financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations.
ops.new: A 2019 study in Health Affairs by Markovitz and colleagues found that because MSSP does not raise an ACO’s benchmark when its patients’ risk scores rise, ACOs have an incentive to shed increasingly sick patients — and beneficiaries at the 95th percentile of risk had a 21.6% chance of exiting MSSP attribution, against 16.0% for beneficiaries at the median. HHS’s 2016 Report to Congress on social risk factors likewise found that providers serving more dual-eligible beneficiaries fared worse under Medicare’s value-based purchasing programs.

ops.old: CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases the spending benchmark for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status — a proxy for overall socioeconomic disadvantage — by up to 3.5%. This adjustment acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively and reduces the financial penalty for serving them. However, the adjustment is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers, both because the 3.5% magnitude is smaller than the evidence base on SDOH cost impact suggests is appropriate, and because low-income subsidy status is an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation. CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors.
ops.new: CMS has moved toward social-risk adjustment in MSSP in steps. The CY2023 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (November 2022) added a health equity adjustment that awards up to 10 bonus points to the quality scores of high-performing ACOs serving large shares of dual-eligible, low-income-subsidy, or high Area Deprivation Index beneficiaries, and created advance investment payments for new low-revenue ACOs in underserved areas. The CY2025 final rule (November 2024) added a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that raises the spending benchmark for ACOs based on their proportion of beneficiaries enrolled in the Part D low-income subsidy or dually eligible for Medicaid. These adjustments acknowledge that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively and reduce the financial penalty for serving them. Health equity researchers argue they remain partial, because low-income subsidy and dual-eligible status are imperfect proxies for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation.
ops.claim: 2022 MSSP final rule "Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment" up to 3.5%; CMS "committed" to ADI/Z-code/CHW-encounter adjustment in the 2026 MSSP final rule
ops.sources: CMS fact sheet, CY2023 PFS final rule — Shared Savings Program (2022-11-01: health equity adjustment, up to 10 bonus points; advance investment payments); CMS fact sheet, CY2025 PFS final rule CMS-1807-F (2024-11-01: Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment based on LIS/dual proportion)
ops.note: Wrong year, invented 3.5% cap, and an invented 2026 commitment; replaced with the two real rules.
